newsitem.title: USA: One in five in U.S. access the Internet - poll.
newsitem.headline: One in five in U.S. access the Internet - poll.

text.p: The number of Americans using the Internet continued to grow dramatically this year, but growth of online service subscribers was flat, a new poll found.
About 18 percent of Americans said they use the Internet as of September, up from 15 percent in April and 14 percent in January, the poll by Louis Harris and Associates found.

About 21 percent subscribe to an online service, like America Online or Compuserve Corp, which may also provides access to the Internet. A January poll also found 21 percent subscribed to online services.
The subscriber base for online services did bounce back from the 17 percent level recorded in April, however.
Online services faced greater competition this year as several big players, such as AT&T Corp, began mass marketing inexpensive Internet access services.
The results of the poll are based on a survey of 1,032 adults at the end of September and have a margin of error of plus or minus three percent, Harris said.
Although more people are accessing the Internet, the poll found people are spending slightly less time there and on online services per week than in April.
Home users said they were online 2.8 hours per week, down from 3 hours a week in April. Business and other users said they were online 1.8 hours a week, down from 2 hours in April.
Users of electronic mail, available to people on the Internet or an online service, rose to 25 percent of all adults in September from 19 percent in January.
People using email at work were more active users, however, sending and receiving 11 messages per week compared to five messages for people electronically posting from home.
About 14 percent said they access the World Wide Web, the graphical portion of the Internet "surfed" with browsers.
That was up from 11 percent in April and January.

The poll reinforced earlier studies showing that computer use is strongly correlated with education. People with college and graduate degrees were twice as likely to use a computer and four times as likely to access the Internet as people who graduated from high school.

Over 80 percent of college and graduate degree holders use a computer and almost 40 percent access the Internet. Among high school graduates, 42 percent use a computer and only eight percent access the Internet.
